Dallas Police Department, UNT Dallas and City of Dallas leadership break ground on the Law Enforcement Training Center, framed by a Komatsu excavator arch, Sept. 3, 2026.
Section 1
The Moment

On the morning of Thursday, September 3, 2026, Dallas Police Chief Daniel Comeaux, city and county leadership and UNT Dallas leadership gathered on a 20-acre stretch of the UNT Dallas campus to break ground on the city's new Law Enforcement Training Center (LETC) — the permanent replacement for a "temporary" academy the department has operated out of a Red Bird–area industrial strip center since 1990. Two Komatsu excavators formed a ceremonial arch over a shovel line of roughly a dozen officials, flanked by DPD patrol vehicles and construction equipment on site.

Allyn's event team counted approximately 450 people in attendance — elected officials, sworn officers, cadets, city and university leadership, stakeholders, donors, project partners (Jacobs, Swinerton, HKS) and sponsors and local media. Separately, the event's QR-linked digital program drove approximately 324 engagement views on its landing page — an additional read on guest interest beyond who showed up.

The day delivered the payoff to a story Dallas has been waiting decades for: DFW media themselves noted the department's new academy had been promised as far back as 1987, and that voters had weighed funding for a permanent facility across several prior bond elections. This time, the dirt actually moved — and Allyn made sure the city saw it happen.

Section 2
What It Means

The LETC is a joint project of the City of Dallas, the Dallas Police Department and the University of North Texas at Dallas, with design and construction partners Jacobs, HKS and Swinerton. Coverage has cited a few different total-cost figures depending on when the story ran and which funding phase it was describing — see Section 3 for the full breakdown, which is one of the more useful insights to come out of this cycle.

For Dallas Police Department: The LETC replaces training space DPD's own chief has publicly called outdated, giving the department a clear, on-record rationale that ran across the day's coverage: "Dallas Police Chief Daniel Comeaux said the department's current training facilities are outdated and in poor condition," per WFAA-TV.

For UNT Dallas: The center embeds police academy training inside a public university campus for the first time in the department's history, with DPD recruits able to earn college credit and the university's Caruth Police Institute relocating to the new facility — a structural, long-term tie between the department and higher education in Southern Dallas.

For the City of Dallas: The groundbreaking gives the city a visible, on-schedule milestone for a major bond-and-grant-funded investment in public safety. Several outlets (KXAS-TV, MSN) paired the celebration with forward-looking coverage of the project's next funding phase — a sign the story has real legs heading into future bond conversations.

For Southern Dallas: Locating the LETC on the UNT Dallas campus places a major civic investment in a part of the city that has historically received less of it — a point Black press outlets (Dallas Weekly, Texas Metro News) picked up independently in their own coverage of the event.

"When I was doing research about coming to the Dallas Police Department, I noticed back in May of 1987 it was in the paper about the Dallas Police Department getting a new academy."
— Dallas Police Chief Daniel Comeaux, KXAS-TV (NBC 5), Sept. 3, 2026
Section 3
How Outlets Reported the Total Project Cost

A story four years in the making has picked up a few different price tags along the way. Lining up every mention side by side surfaces a genuinely useful insight: coverage has cited four total-cost figures, each tied to a different point in the project's funding timeline.

Figure CitedSourceWhenBasis Given
$80 millionUNT DallasFunding-announcement phase, pre-groundbreaking$10M Communities Foundation of Texas gift + $20M state legislature (2023) + $50M planned in the city bond package
$100–million+Dallas WeeklyCoverage following the groundbreaking$50M 2024 Dallas Bond Program + $25M in state grants + $30M+ from private donors and foundations
$140 millionFOX 4 (online video)Sept. 3, 2026 (event day)Not itemized in the segment
$227 millionWFAA-TV; CW 33 (broadcast); Correctional NewsSept. 3–4, 2026 (event day)Cited as the cost of the full 20-acre campus/facility
$82 million (to complete)Michael Igo, former interim Dallas police chief, in the Dallas Morning NewsSept. 15, 2026 (Proposition A campaign)The remaining ask on the November 2026 ballot — Proposition A would provide $82M to finish LETC construction
$80M, $100M+ and $140M all roughly track the funding stack as it was built up over time — philanthropic gift, then state grant, then bond commitments, then private fundraising. $227M, cited at groundbreaking itself, is the largest figure and the one now most anchored in the public record. And the go-forward number has an answer: Proposition A, on the November 2026 ballot, would provide the $82M needed to complete construction.
One more distinction worth keeping straight for future coverage: the Dallas Morning News piece "Donors can put their names on Dallas' new police academy" also cites a $443 million bond proposition, of which $149 million would fund a different, related facility — a Public Safety Training Complex at Dallas Executive Airport, itself estimated at ~$170 million. Michael Igo's Sept. 15 piece confirms that same $149M figure sits alongside the $82M LETC ask, both under Proposition A. The airport complex is a separate project from the LETC at UNT Dallas.

Section 5
Execution & Turnout
Chief Comeaux addresses the tented audience; the screen recognizes sponsors.
01
A Live Groundbreaking, On a Working Construction Site
The run of show centered on a live groundbreaking format — a shovel line, a ceremonial excavator arch, tented seating and a dedicated press area — staged on an active construction site, with a program built to work for both dignitaries and a full broadcast press pool.
02
A Shovel Line for 60+ Stakeholders and Nearly 20 Elected Officials
13 separate shovel-line photos captured more than 60 stakeholders in total (each grouping running five to twenty people), sequencing federal, state, county and city officials alongside DPD, UNT Dallas and project-partner leadership for the cameras. Close to 20 sitting elected officials attended in person, spanning the Texas Senate and House, Dallas County Commissioners Court and Dallas City Council, with two U.S. Senate offices represented by staff.
State Senate: Sen. Royce West, Sen. Bob Hall, Sen. Nathan Johnson, Sen. Tan Parker.
State House: Rep. Toni Rose, Rep. Morgan Meyer, Rep. Rhetta Bowers, Rep. Terry Meza; staff for Rep. Rafael Anchía.
Dallas County: County Commissioner John Wiley Price, Dallas County Judge Clay Jenkins.
City of Dallas: Mayor Eric Johnson, Mayor Pro Tem Jaime Reséndez and Councilmembers Bill Roth, Gay Donnell Willis, Maxie Johnson, Cara Mendelsohn, Paul Ridley, Jesse Moreno, Lorie Blair and Kathy Stewart.
Federal: staff representing Sen. Ted Cruz and Sen. John Cornyn.
03
Same-Day Coverage Across Every Major DFW Outlet
Every major Dallas-Fort Worth broadcast outlet — NBC 5, FOX 4, WFAA (ABC), CBS Texas, CW33 and KRLD-AM — carried the story the same day, several with live, on-site interviews with Chief Comeaux. That kind of same-day, all-outlet turnout reflects advance media logistics and relationships, not organic pickup.
04
Guest Engagement, Beyond the Headcount
Beyond the ~450 attendees counted on-site, the event's QR-linked digital program logged approximately 324 landing-page views — a clear signal that interest in the LETC story reached beyond the people who attended in person.
Section 6
Sponsorships Secured

To help underwrite the groundbreaking, the LETC Task Force asked local business and civic partners to sponsor the event across four recognition levels, with a $40,000 production goal. Eight sponsors — Atmos, Billingsley, Central Market, Citizens Council, Jacobs, Oncor, Swinerton and Walmart — came in at a combined $49,500, exceeding that goal. No sponsor took the event's exclusive $15,000 Presenting Sponsor tier.
